大中臣氏（おおなかとみし）は古代の祭祀貴族。 中臣鎌足が藤原姓を賜った後、その子藤原不比等以外の中臣氏は大中臣氏と称するようになる。
大中臣氏の中で最も力を振るったのは'''大中臣清麻呂'''（[[位階|正二位]]・[[右大臣]]）（702年～788年）の系統で、[[神祇官|神祇伯]]や[[伊勢]][[祭主]]を世襲した。平安時代の[[大中臣能宣]]とその[[子大中臣輔親]]そその孫[[伊勢大輔]]は歌人としても事績を残している。
[[平安中期]]以降[[白川氏]]が[[神祇官|神祇伯]]を世襲するようになると、[[伊勢]][[祭主]]及び[[神祇大副]]を世襲するようになる。
子孫は江戸時代に[[藤波家]]を称するようになる。

[[藤原鎌足|中臣鎌足]]が[[藤原]]姓を賜った後、その子[[藤原不比等]]が幼かったため、鎌足の甥で婿養子とも言われる[[中臣意美麻呂]]が暫定的に[[藤原氏]]を継いだ。後に、不比等の成長を待ち、正式に[[文武天皇]]の命令によって改めて鎌足の嫡男として不比等とその子孫のみに藤原姓を許し、他の者は[[中臣氏]]に復するように命じられて意美麻呂も中臣姓に戻る。意美麻呂は不比等の後押しで[[中納言]]に昇進した。意美麻呂の息子である[[大中臣清麻呂]]（[[位階|正二位]]・[[右大臣]]）（702年～788年）は、[[神護景雲]]3年（[[769年]]）6月に「大中臣朝臣」を下賜されて、以後その子孫は「大中臣氏」と称した。
また、後には中臣氏の嫡流あるいはそれに近いとされた「三門」（『中臣氏系図』）と呼ばれる家々<ref>「三門」は[[中臣可多能祜]]の男子3名の末裔の事で[[中臣御食子]]の子孫（ただし、鎌足は藤原氏となったため、その弟[[中臣垂目|垂目]]の子孫となる）を「第一門」、[[中臣国子]]の子孫を「第二門」、[[中臣糠手子]]の子孫を「第三門」と称した。</ref>があったが、平安時代に入るとこれらの家々にに対しても大中臣氏の名乗りが許されるようになった<ref>延暦16年（797年）から翌年にかけて「第一門」「第二門」（清麻呂子孫 ）を除くにも大中臣朝臣が与えられ、遅れて元慶元年（877年）には「第三門」にも大中臣朝臣が与えられた。</ref>。
大中臣氏の中で最も力を振るったのは嫡流とされた清麻呂の系統で、[[神祇官|神祇伯]]や[[伊勢神宮|伊勢]][[祭主]]を世襲した。平安時代の[[大中臣能宣]]とその子[[大中臣輔親]]その孫[[伊勢大輔]]は[[歌人]]としても事績を残している。
だが、平安時代中期の[[中臣逸志]]<ref>逸志は「第三門」では唯一の神祇伯であり、「第三門」への大中臣朝臣賜姓もその功績によるところとされている。</ref>を最後に中臣氏（大中臣氏）の[[神祇官|神祇伯]]は姿を消し、代わって[[白川家]]が[[神祇官|神祇伯]]を世襲するようになると、伊勢祭主及び[[神祇官|神祇大副]]を世襲するようになる。また、地方の有力神社の神職も掌握するようになる。
嫡流子孫は[[江戸時代]]に[[藤波家]]を称するようになる。

[[桐村氏]]（[[武家]]） }} '''大中臣氏'''（おおなかとみし）は[[日本]][[古代]]の中央政権において[[祭祀]]をつかさどった[[貴族]]。 __TOC__{{-}} == 概要 == [[藤原鎌足|中臣鎌足]]が藤原姓を賜った後、その子[[藤原不比等]]が幼かったため、鎌足の[[おい|甥]]で[[婿養子]]とも言われる[[中臣意美麻呂]]が暫定的に[[藤原氏]]を継いだ。後に、不比等の成長を待ち、正式に[[文武天皇]]の命令によって改めて鎌足の嫡男として不比等とその子孫のみに藤原姓を許し、他の者は[[中臣氏]]に復するように命じられて意美麻呂も中臣姓に戻る。意美麻呂は不比等の後押しで[[中納言]]に昇進した。意美麻呂の息子である[[大中臣清麻呂]]（[[正二位]]・[[右大臣]]、[[702年]] - [[788年]]）は、[[神護景雲]]3年（[[769年]]）6月に「大中臣朝臣」を賜姓されて、以後その子孫は「大中臣氏」と称した。 また、後には中臣氏の[[嫡流]]あるいはそれに近いとされた「三門」（『中臣氏系図』）と呼ばれる家々「三門」は[[中臣可多能祜]]の男子3名の末裔の事で[[中臣御食子]]の子孫（ただし、鎌足は藤原氏となったため、その弟[[中臣垂目|垂目]]の子孫となる）を「第一門」、[[中臣国子]]の子孫を「第二門」、[[中臣糠手子]]の子孫を「第三門」と称した。があったが、[[平安時代]]に入るとこれらの家々に対しても大中臣氏の名乗りが許されるようになった[[延暦]]16年（[[797年]]）から翌年にかけて「第一門」「第二門」（清麻呂子孫を除く）にも大中臣朝臣が与えられ、遅れて[[元慶]]元年（[[877年]]）には「第三門」にも大中臣朝臣が与えられた。。 大中臣氏の中で最も力を振るったのは[[嫡流]]とされた清麻呂の系統で、[[神祇官|神祇伯]]や[[祭主|伊勢祭主]]を世襲した。[[平安時代]]の[[大中臣能宣]]とその子[[大中臣輔親]]その孫[[伊勢大輔]]は[[歌人]]としても事績を残している。 だが、[[平安時代]]中期の[[中臣逸志]]逸志は「第三門」では唯一の神祇伯であり、「第三門」への大中臣朝臣賜姓もその功績によるところとされている。を最後に中臣氏（大中臣氏）の神祇伯は姿を消し、代わって[[白川家]]が神祇伯を世襲するようになると、伊勢祭主及び[[神祇官|神祇大副]]を世襲するようになる。また、地方の有力神社の神職も掌握するようになる。 [[嫡流]]子孫は[[江戸時代]]に[[藤波家]]を称するようになる。 == 脚注 == == 参考文献 == * 中村英重「中臣氏と家門」（所収:吉村武彦 編『律令制国家と古代社会の詳細』（[[塙書房]]、{{jdate|2005}}） ISBN 978-4-8273-1196-9） == 関連項目 == * [[中臣氏]] * [[神祇官]] * [[祭主]] * [[藤波家]] == 外部リンク == * [http://www.myj7000.jp-biz.net/clan/02/021/02109.htm 日本の苗字7000傑 姓氏類別大観 中臣氏／大中臣氏【1】] {{ja icon}} * [http://www.myj7000.jp-biz.net/clan/02/020/02000.htm 日本の苗字7000傑 姓氏類別大観 藤原氏総括] {{ja icon}} * [http://shushen.hp.infoseek.co.jp/keihu/sizokugairan/fujiwarag.htm 藤原氏概説] {{ja icon}} {{japanese-history-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:おおなかとみし}} [[Category:中臣氏|*]] [[Category:大中臣氏|*]] [[Category:日本の氏族]] [[Category:本姓|おおなかとみ]]

[[Naka clan]] (samurai)
[[Nakagori clan]] (samurai)
[[Kanayama clan]] (samurai)
[[Kirihara clan]] (samurai)
[[Komata clan#Branch from Ōnakatomi|Komata clan]] (samurai)
[[Izumi Wada clan]] (samurai)
[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==
Genealogy of the Ōnakatomi Clan

They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

[[Komata clan#Branch from Ōnakatomi|Komata clan]] (samurai)
[[Izumi Wada clan]] (samurai)
[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==
Genealogy of the Ōnakatomi Clan

They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==
Genealogy of the Ōnakatomi Clan

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==

{{Ancient Japanese clans | clan_name = 大中臣氏 | image = | clan_name_in_japanese = 大中臣[[朝臣]] | founder = | origin = [[中臣氏]] | ancestor = [[大中臣清麻呂]] | classification = [[Shinbetsu]] ([[Amatsukami]]) | main_location = [[Yamashiro Province]], etc. | notable_people = [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]]
[[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]]
[[Ise no Taifu]] | descendants = '''[[Fujinami family (Ōnakatomi clan)|Fujinami family]]''' ([[kuge]] and [[kazoku]])
[[Naka clan]] (samurai)
[[Nakagori clan]] (samurai)
[[Kanayama clan]] (samurai)
[[Kirihara clan]] (samurai)
[[Komata clan#Branch from Ōnakatomi|Komata clan]] (samurai)
[[Izumi Wada clan]] (samurai)
[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Jingikan|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[Edo period]]. == Genealogy ==
Genealogy of the Ōnakatomi Clan

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Kirihara clan]] (samurai)

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==
