[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After [[:en:Fujiwara no Kamatari|Fujiwara no Kamatari]] of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son [[:en:Fujiwara no Fuhito|Fujiwara no Fuhito]] was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his [[:en:Son-in-law|Son-in-law]], temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of [[:en:Chūnagon|Chūnagon]] (Middle Councilor). His son [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro]] gained prominence during the [[:en:Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion]] in 764, supporting [[:en:Empress Kōken|Empress Kōken]] (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]], families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like [[:en:Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu]] and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as [[:en:Ise no Taifu|Ise no Taifu]], a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]]. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

{{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu}} | descendants = '''[[Fujinami family (Ōnakatomi clan)|Fujinami family]]''' ([[kuge]] and [[kazoku]])

[[Nakagori clan]] (samurai)

[[Kirihara clan]] (samurai)
[[Komata clan#Branch from Ōnakatomi|Komata clan]] (samurai)
[[Izumi Wada clan]] (samurai)
[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==

[[Aiba clan]] (samurai) }} The '''Ōnakatomi clan''' (大中臣氏) was an ancient Japanese clan whose name derives from the use of "Ōnakatomi" as a surname. They were aristocrats and priests who oversaw [[Shinto]] rituals in the central government during ancient Japan. == Overview == After {{ill|Fujiwara no Kamatari|en|Fujiwara no Kamatari|WD=Q433995|lt=Fujiwara no Kamatari|1=Fujiwara no Kamatari}} of the [[Nakatomi clan]] was granted the surname "Fujiwara," his son {{ill|Fujiwara no Fuhito|en|Fujiwara no Fuhito|WD=Q177517|lt=Fujiwara no Fuhito|1=Fujiwara no Fuhito}} was still a child. Kamatari’s nephew [[Nakatomi no Omimaro]], who was also his {{ill|Son-in-law|en|Son-in-law|WD=Q3752578|lt=Son-in-law|1=Son-in-law}}, temporarily succeeded as the head of the Fujiwara clan. Later, Emperor [[Monmu]] officially restored the Fujiwara surname solely to Kamatari's descendants, prompting Omimaro and others to revert to the Nakatomi surname. Despite this, Omimaro rose to the position of {{ill|Chūnagon|en|Chūnagon|WD=Q1185382|lt=Chūnagon|1=Chūnagon}} (Middle Councilor). His son {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|en|Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|WD=Q11431854|lt=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro|1=Ōnakatomi no Kiyomaro}} gained prominence during the {{ill|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|en|Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|WD=Q11623017|lt=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion|1=Fujiwara no Nakamaro Rebellion}} in 764, supporting {{ill|Empress Kōken|en|Empress Kōken|WD=Q232955|lt=Empress Kōken|1=Empress Kōken}} (later Empress Shōtoku) and was rewarded with the surname "Ōnakatomi" in 769. Kiyomaro eventually rose to [[Senior Second Rank]] and [[:en:Udaijin|Udaijin]] (Right Minister). During the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|WD=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}}, families within the Nakatomi clan were categorized into three houses known as the "Three Gates" ("Sanmon") as recorded in the "Nakatomi Genealogy.""Sanmon" refers to the three male descendants of [[Nakatomi no Katanoho]], [[Nakatomi no Mikeko]], and [[Nakatomi no Kokateko]]. By the late 8th century, those in close relation to Kiyomaro adopted the name "Ōnakatomi." The Ōnakatomi clan’s most influential branch, stemming from Kiyomaro, held hereditary positions as [[Department of Divinities|Jingi-haku]] (Head of Shinto Affairs) and [[:en:Saishu|Saishu]] (Chief Priest of the Ise Grand Shrine). Prominent figures include poets like {{ill|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|en|Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|WD=Q1273650|lt=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu|1=Ōnakatomi no Yoshinobu}} and [[Ōnakatomi no Suketomo]], as well as {{ill|Ise no Taifu|en|Ise no Taifu|WD=Q3072228|lt=Ise no Taifu|1=Ise no Taifu}}, a renowned female poet. By the late Heian period, the [[Shirakawa clan]] succeeded the Ōnakatomi as hereditary holders of the Jingi-haku office. The remaining members of the clan focused on regional shrine leadership and priesthood. The main lineage eventually became known as the [[Fujinami family]], a prominent court family in the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}}. ==Family tree==
